source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: When all moves can be seen but one exact move is right, a beginner cannot tell a helpful move from a useless one and plays like chance.
pros: An expert can play every game without a mistake.
Nothing is hidden.
cons: A beginner has no way to tell if a move helped.
Beginner and expert play very different games.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: When players can offer to double the stakes mid-game, a leader's confidence is tested by the other player's answer.
pros: The leader can use the lead to press on.
The other player may leave and keep their loss small.
cons: A player behind may fold too soon.
The money at risk changes how players think.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: A bid made before a hand of tricks commits the bidder, and the hand shows whether the bid is kept. The cost of failing is known in advance.
pros: Players say aloud how sure they are of their cards
The bidder has a clear aim for the whole hand
cons: A failed bid can wipe out points won during the hand
A player with few high cards has little to bid, so one player often carries the hand

source.ref: Fitzsimmons, T. and Liflander, P. (1996). The everything games book: hundreds of classic games for all ages. Holbrook, MA: Adams Media. ISBN 978-1-55850-643-5.

pairs.tendency: When bids are made in points and scores count down to nothing, a bid that is made moves a player towards the finish and a failed bid moves them back.
pros: Every hand moves each player's distance from the end
A set-back is easy to see and to count
cons: A sold bid moves the seller forward before any card is played
A failed hand throws away the points won in it

source.ref: Fitzsimmons, T. and Liflander, P. (1996). The everything games book: hundreds of classic games for all ages. Holbrook, MA: Adams Media. ISBN 978-1-55850-643-5.

pairs.tendency: When each player gets one bid in turn and the last speaker may sell or refuse, the order of speaking shapes the bids.
pros: Each player speaks once, so the auction ends quickly
The last speaker hears every bid before choosing
cons: Early bidders have to bid without hearing the others
The last speaker may refuse every bid and keep the right

source.ref: Fitzsimmons, T. and Liflander, P. (1996). The everything games book: hundreds of classic games for all ages. Holbrook, MA: Adams Media. ISBN 978-1-55850-643-5.

pairs.tendency: When a player may beg after a low-card deal, the dealer chooses between giving a point and dealing new cards to both players.
pros: A low deal is not final
The dealer has a choice to make at every beg
cons: The new cards may be no higher than the old ones
Each beg either costs a point or changes the hand for both players

source.ref: Fitzsimmons, T. and Liflander, P. (1996). The everything games book: hundreds of classic games for all ages. Holbrook, MA: Adams Media. ISBN 978-1-55850-643-5.

pairs.tendency: When points sit on cards that the trick winner collects, a player can send points to a chosen rival or away from a leader.
pros: Players with no hope of scoring can still shape who gains
Players can see which person each point goes to
cons: A player may spend a hand helping one rival instead of playing for themselves
The player in front can find points kept from them

source.ref: Fitzsimmons, T. and Liflander, P. (1996). The everything games book: hundreds of classic games for all ages. Holbrook, MA: Adams Media. ISBN 978-1-55850-643-5.

pairs.tendency: When the stock lies face up and each player refills their hand from it, only the cards in hand stay secret.
pros: Players can plan for cards they can see coming
Counting the stock takes no extra effort
cons: The planning gain ends once the stock is used up
Players still have to guess what the other hand holds

source.ref: Fitzsimmons, T. and Liflander, P. (1996). The everything games book: hundreds of classic games for all ages. Holbrook, MA: Adams Media. ISBN 978-1-55850-643-5.

pairs.tendency: When a higher bid pays more and each missing trick costs more, players weigh how far to go before the hand starts.
pros: A cautious bid and a bold bid both stay open
A bold bid that succeeds pays more
cons: A failed bid costs more with each trick missed
A failed bid also doubles the pool

source.ref: Fitzsimmons, T. and Liflander, P. (1996). The everything games book: hundreds of classic games for all ages. Holbrook, MA: Adams Media. ISBN 978-1-55850-643-5.

pairs.tendency: In Boston, once a bid is made the other three players all play against the bidder, so the auction settles who stands against whom.
pros: Sides are settled by the bidding, with no secret roles
The three opponents share one clear aim
cons: One player faces three and carries the whole loss
A failed bidder pays each of the other players

source.ref: Fitzsimmons, T. and Liflander, P. (1996). The everything games book: hundreds of classic games for all ages. Holbrook, MA: Adams Media. ISBN 978-1-55850-643-5.

A long ladder of bids takes time to learn

pros: Choices are quick, so the game moves fast

cons: A player holding many cards of one suit can be stuck for turns

Hands are thrown in when nobody wants to play alone

source.ref: Fitzsimmons, T. and Liflander, P. (1996). The everything games book: hundreds of classic games for all ages. Holbrook, MA: Adams Media. ISBN 978-1-55850-643-5.

source.ref: Fitzsimmons, T. and Liflander, P. (1996). The everything games book: hundreds of classic games for all ages. Holbrook, MA: Adams Media. ISBN 978-1-55850-643-5.

cons: Points pile up on one player.

source.ref: Fitzsimmons, T. and Liflander, P. (1996). The everything games book: hundreds of classic games for all ages. Holbrook, MA: Adams Media. ISBN 978-1-55850-643-5.

Scores can swing sharply from one deal to the next

pairs.tendency: In Hearts, once a player has taken a penalty card, the others often work together to load more onto the same person.
pros: A player who is ahead is soon noticed by the others
Cards can be aimed at one person on purpose
cons: One player can be picked on for several deals
An early mistake can snowball

pros: Every deal opens with a choice of which cards to pass

cons: Your neighbour gets the cards you did not want
You pick cards before you see what you will get

pros: A bold plan can turn an unlucky deal into a large gain

Going for it means giving up the safe play

pairs.tendency: In Solo, whoever holds the ace the caller names becomes a secret partner, and the pair is known only when the ace is played.
pros: Opponents have to guess who is on the caller's side

cons: A partner who helps too openly shows the link
The caller cannot tell the partner what to do

Rivals cannot tell how many high cards you hold

A player with many high cards may have to lose tricks on purpose

A single miss scores nothing for the whole deal

Waiting is long when the hands are large

A high-ranked set can win more when others keep betting
cons: A bluff that is called loses chips
Players who never bet lose to those who do

pairs.tendency: Poker hands are ranked sets, such as pairs and runs, and nobody sees another player's set until the showdown.
pros: Rarer sets beat more common ones

Drawing back to five keeps options open

Ending the turn on a side stack wastes a chance to play on

A side stack cannot be moved once it is started

cons: The card thrown away cannot be looked at again
The next card may turn out to be less useful

A hand that is checked on purpose hides its worth until later

A hand's worth changes with how many players remain in the pot

The number of players left changes what a hand is worth

cons: A player who cannot follow suit has to pick up every card in the trick.
Taking up a trick sets a player back by several cards at once.

source.ref: Morehead, A. H. and Mott-Smith, G. (eds) (1983). Hoyle's rules of games: descriptions of indoor games of skill and chance, with advice on skillful play. 2nd revised edition. New York: Signet. ISBN 978-0-451-16309-7.

pairs.tendency: Two opponents team up against one contractor, yet each keeps a separate score for the tricks that player wins.
pros: Both opponents share the aim of defeating the contract.
Each still gains from winning tricks, so neither is only a helper.
cons: Each opponent's own score depends on tricks they win, which can pull them away from the shared aim.
Neither opponent can see the other's hand, so help is guesswork.

source.ref: Morehead, A. H. and Mott-Smith, G. (eds) (1983). Hoyle's rules of games: descriptions of indoor games of skill and chance, with advice on skillful play. 2nd revised edition. New York: Signet. ISBN 978-0-451-16309-7.

pairs.tendency: Scoring for matched cards, such as a king and queen of one suit, sits beside scoring for tricks won.
pros: A hand can earn points before a single card is led.
A player has two ways to gain points and chooses between them.
cons: Cards held back for a match may be cards the player would rather lead.
Rules about which matches may be counted at once grow long.

source.ref: Morehead, A. H. and Mott-Smith, G. (eds) (1983). Hoyle's rules of games: descriptions of indoor games of skill and chance, with advice on skillful play. 2nd revised edition. New York: Signet. ISBN 978-0-451-16309-7.

pairs.tendency: A high trump is sold to the highest bidder while other cards are face down, so each price is a guess.
pros: Buyers pay for a chance, so each sale is a bet on what is hidden.
A player can buy up unturned cards to make sure of winning the pool.
cons: A buyer can pay a high price and still lose to a card not yet turned.
The price goes to the seller, not the pool, so sellers gain even when buyers lose.

source.ref: Morehead, A. H. and Mott-Smith, G. (eds) (1983). Hoyle's rules of games: descriptions of indoor games of skill and chance, with advice on skillful play. 2nd revised edition. New York: Signet. ISBN 978-0-451-16309-7.

pairs.tendency: When players choose how many chips to risk on one unseen card, counting the cards already seen changes the odds of each bet.
pros: A player can bet small when the odds are against the player and bigger when they favour the player.
A bet can be anything from one chip to the whole pot, so one card can swing a lot.
cons: Every bet still rests on a single unseen card.
Keeping count of cards takes attention, and the odds often stay close to even.

source.ref: Morehead, A. H. and Mott-Smith, G. (eds) (1983). Hoyle's rules of games: descriptions of indoor games of skill and chance, with advice on skillful play. 2nd revised edition. New York: Signet. ISBN 978-0-451-16309-7.

pairs.tendency: Each player gives two cards to a crib owned by one player, so every deal is a choice between keeping points and denying them.
pros: The same cards are kept or given up differently depending on whose crib it is.
Players can lay away cards far apart in rank to starve an opponent's crib.
cons: The card turned up after the choice can raise or spoil the hand that was kept.
A player sometimes has to split a pair or a run to protect the crib.

source.ref: Morehead, A. H. and Mott-Smith, G. (eds) (1983). Hoyle's rules of games: descriptions of indoor games of skill and chance, with advice on skillful play. 2nd revised edition. New York: Signet. ISBN 978-0-451-16309-7.

pairs.tendency: When players add cards to one shared running total, each card played changes which scores the next player can make.
pros: A play can block a fifteen or a run before the other player reaches it.
Players read what the other might hold from the total on the table.
cons: There is no defence against a pair, so some scores cannot be stopped.
A card that blocks one score may leave the player's own cards short for the call of go.

source.ref: Morehead, A. H. and Mott-Smith, G. (eds) (1983). Hoyle's rules of games: descriptions of indoor games of skill and chance, with advice on skillful play. 2nd revised edition. New York: Signet. ISBN 978-0-451-16309-7.

pairs.tendency: Face cards can only be taken by a matching card, so what a player holds in the last hand shows where the match is.
pros: A player who remembers the cards seen can work out what the opponent holds.
Keeping a card for the last play gives first chance at it next deal.
cons: Following every card takes a lot of memory and attention.
A card kept too long may be lost to a build the opponent makes.

source.ref: Morehead, A. H. and Mott-Smith, G. (eds) (1983). Hoyle's rules of games: descriptions of indoor games of skill and chance, with advice on skillful play. 2nd revised edition. New York: Signet. ISBN 978-0-451-16309-7.

pairs.tendency: A player who lays a card on table cards to make a total keeps a card in hand that can take it.
pros: A build ties up a card in the hand, so the opponent can guess what the player holds.
A build can be increased or doubled, changing which card takes it.
cons: An opponent who holds the right card can capture the whole build.
A build that cannot be taken in costs the builder a point.

source.ref: Morehead, A. H. and Mott-Smith, G. (eds) (1983). Hoyle's rules of games: descriptions of indoor games of skill and chance, with advice on skillful play. 2nd revised edition. New York: Signet. ISBN 978-0-451-16309-7.

pairs.tendency: When players draw and discard to gather one suit and the lowest hand pays a chip, players drop out as chips run out.
pros: Players stay in until their chips are gone, and may play on once after that.
Knocking ends the hand early for a player who thinks the hand is high enough.
cons: Several players can share the lowest count and all pay at once.
A player who pays the last chip can be out on the next low hand.

source.ref: Morehead, A. H. and Mott-Smith, G. (eds) (1983). Hoyle's rules of games: descriptions of indoor games of skill and chance, with advice on skillful play. 2nd revised edition. New York: Signet. ISBN 978-0-451-16309-7.

pairs.tendency: Each player draws against the dealer and loses on passing 21, so the dealer's shown card guides how far each player risks.
pros: A player can stop at any time, so the risk is chosen.
The dealer's shown card gives something to judge each draw by.
cons: A player who goes over loses at once, even if the dealer later goes over too.
A dealer facing many players who stood may have to draw and go over.

source.ref: Morehead, A. H. and Mott-Smith, G. (eds) (1983). Hoyle's rules of games: descriptions of indoor games of skill and chance, with advice on skillful play. 2nd revised edition. New York: Signet. ISBN 978-0-451-16309-7.

pairs.tendency: When a player may swap a card with the neighbour, who has to accept, an unwanted card travels round the table.
pros: A turn is quick: look, keep or swap, then pass on.
Players holding a high card are pushed to hand it on.
cons: A swap decides little, because most of the result comes from the card dealt.
In one version a king cannot be swapped, so its holder takes no part.

source.ref: Morehead, A. H. and Mott-Smith, G. (eds) (1983). Hoyle's rules of games: descriptions of indoor games of skill and chance, with advice on skillful play. 2nd revised edition. New York: Signet. ISBN 978-0-451-16309-7.

pairs.tendency: Cards in a row may only move onto a card of the same suit or rank, so the deal forces nearly every move.
pros: A game finishes in a few minutes.
The few real choices are easy to see.
cons: A player almost always loses, so winning is rare.
Reducing the number of piles is the only skill left.

source.ref: Morehead, A. H. and Mott-Smith, G. (eds) (1983). Hoyle's rules of games: descriptions of indoor games of skill and chance, with advice on skillful play. 2nd revised edition. New York: Signet. ISBN 978-0-451-16309-7.

pairs.tendency: When cards are built down in sequence and empty spaces let a player rearrange piles, skill can offset some luck.
pros: Empty spaces let a player plan and swap cards between piles.
Face-down cards turn up as piles are cleared, so a move can open more moves.
cons: A new row of cards cannot be dealt until every space is filled.
Moving a king into a space can use up the most useful space.

source.ref: Morehead, A. H. and Mott-Smith, G. (eds) (1983). Hoyle's rules of games: descriptions of indoor games of skill and chance, with advice on skillful play. 2nd revised edition. New York: Signet. ISBN 978-0-451-16309-7.

pairs.tendency: Players each have a pack and tableau and play onto shared ace piles at once, and the first to empty the reserve wins.
pros: Nobody waits, so the game moves fast.
A card played on a shared pile helps every player.
cons: With no turns, players have to agree how to settle disputes.
Play can become disorderly if the rules of procedure are loose.

source.ref: Morehead, A. H. and Mott-Smith, G. (eds) (1983). Hoyle's rules of games: descriptions of indoor games of skill and chance, with advice on skillful play. 2nd revised edition. New York: Signet. ISBN 978-0-451-16309-7.

pairs.tendency: When two players build on their own piles and may place cards on the opponent's stock, getting rid of cards is also an attack.
pros: Placing a card on the opponent's pile clears the player's own pile.
Strict order of play settles who may do what and when.
cons: A player who breaks the order loses the turn.
The opponent's pile can be built on only in suit and sequence.

source.ref: Morehead, A. H. and Mott-Smith, G. (eds) (1983). Hoyle's rules of games: descriptions of indoor games of skill and chance, with advice on skillful play. 2nd revised edition. New York: Signet. ISBN 978-0-451-16309-7.

pairs.tendency: When the bank is sold by auction and all others may bet against it, the bid sets how much they can win or lose.
pros: The auction picks the player willing to carry the most risk.
Any player may cover part or all of the bank.
cons: A banker who loses passes the bank to another player.
The banker is never liable beyond the amount of the bank.

source.ref: Morehead, A. H. and Mott-Smith, G. (eds) (1983). Hoyle's rules of games: descriptions of indoor games of skill and chance, with advice on skillful play. 2nd revised edition. New York: Signet. ISBN 978-0-451-16309-7.

pairs.tendency: Players have private boards and a referee who only says no, check or capture, so they work out hidden pieces from the answers.
pros: An illegal try tells a player that a piece blocks the way.
A capture announcement tells where, but not what was taken.
cons: Someone has to act as referee and keep the true position on a third board.
The game needs three boards and two players kept apart.

source.ref: Morehead, A. H. and Mott-Smith, G. (eds) (1983). Hoyle's rules of games: descriptions of indoor games of skill and chance, with advice on skillful play. 2nd revised edition. New York: Signet. ISBN 978-0-451-16309-7.

pairs.tendency: When all bets are placed against a bank and a wheel decides each result, no betting system changes the result in the long run.
pros: Anyone near the table can join in.
Each bet has a stated payout, so the odds are open.
cons: Skill in choosing bets does not change the long-run outcome.
The bank keeps a fixed share of all bets in the long run.

source.ref: Morehead, A. H. and Mott-Smith, G. (eds) (1983). Hoyle's rules of games: descriptions of indoor games of skill and chance, with advice on skillful play. 2nd revised edition. New York: Signet. ISBN 978-0-451-16309-7.

pairs.tendency: When two partners sit opposite each other but one partner takes in all the cards, the partners mostly pool their scores.
pros: Scores from both partners are added together.
The game stays easy to run with four players.
cons: The play gives the partners little to do together.
One partner's play counts for the whole side.

source.ref: Morehead, A. H. and Mott-Smith, G. (eds) (1983). Hoyle's rules of games: descriptions of indoor games of skill and chance, with advice on skillful play. 2nd revised edition. New York: Signet. ISBN 978-0-451-16309-7.

pairs.tendency: Two players each play the same solitaire with their own pack and compare scores, so neither can affect the other's game.
pros: Neither player waits for the other.
Scores are easy to compare, and nine holes can be summed.
cons: Players cannot help or block each other.
A player's result depends only on their own pack and moves.

source.ref: Morehead, A. H. and Mott-Smith, G. (eds) (1983). Hoyle's rules of games: descriptions of indoor games of skill and chance, with advice on skillful play. 2nd revised edition. New York: Signet. ISBN 978-0-451-16309-7.

pairs.tendency: With every mark in view and a row as the aim, the player who starts can force a win unless a rule limits them.
pros: The aim is plain and anyone can see it
Every threat is open to both players
cons: The first player may hold a forced win
A smaller board or a limit on pieces is the way to keep it open

source.ref: Morehead, A. H. and Mott-Smith, G. (eds) (1983). Hoyle's rules of games: descriptions of indoor games of skill and chance, with advice on skillful play. 2nd revised edition. New York: Signet. ISBN 978-0-451-16309-7.

pairs.tendency: On a tiny grid with no luck, careful players tend to draw, so only beginners still win games.
pros: Quick to learn and quick to finish
The whole board is easy to see at once
cons: Careful play on both sides tends to end level
Interest fades once players know the right reply

source.ref: Morehead, A. H. and Mott-Smith, G. (eds) (1983). Hoyle's rules of games: descriptions of indoor games of skill and chance, with advice on skillful play. 2nd revised edition. New York: Signet. ISBN 978-0-451-16309-7.

pairs.tendency: With nothing hidden and nothing rolled, practised players drew so often that organisers added a random start.
pros: Every result comes from choices both players can see
Mistakes are easy to find afterwards
cons: Practised players draw in many games
A chance opening had to be added to separate them

source.ref: Morehead, A. H. and Mott-Smith, G. (eds) (1983). Hoyle's rules of games: descriptions of indoor games of skill and chance, with advice on skillful play. 2nd revised edition. New York: Signet. ISBN 978-0-451-16309-7.

pairs.tendency: A rule letting players raise the stake gave Backgammon more room for skill on top of the dice.
pros: Choosing how to split a roll between pieces
Choosing when to double or give up
cons: A low roll still costs whole turns
The stake can grow fast once doubling starts

source.ref: Morehead, A. H. and Mott-Smith, G. (eds) (1983). Hoyle's rules of games: descriptions of indoor games of skill and chance, with advice on skillful play. 2nd revised edition. New York: Signet. ISBN 978-0-451-16309-7.

pairs.tendency: Sending an opponent's piece back to the start costs them turns, so one hit can swing a race.
pros: A hit turns a plain race into a fight
A lone piece becomes a risk to leave out
cons: Each hit costs its owner one to four turns
A player far behind may hold pieces back to hit later

source.ref: Morehead, A. H. and Mott-Smith, G. (eds) (1983). Hoyle's rules of games: descriptions of indoor games of skill and chance, with advice on skillful play. 2nd revised edition. New York: Signet. ISBN 978-0-451-16309-7.

pairs.tendency: Once you choose to roll again you have to claim more than your opponent did, so you cannot back out by calling the bluff.
pros: Rolling again can improve a low hand
A claim can be raised without showing the dice
cons: Rolling again closes the way to a challenge
Each raise makes doubt more tempting for the next player

source.ref: Morehead, A. H. and Mott-Smith, G. (eds) (1983). Hoyle's rules of games: descriptions of indoor games of skill and chance, with advice on skillful play. 2nd revised edition. New York: Signet. ISBN 978-0-451-16309-7.

pairs.tendency: When the first to empty their hand wins, cheating early and telling the truth near the end tends to pay.
pros: Early lies cost little
The plan is easy to describe
cons: The last cards are always doubted
A player short of a rank may have to doubt to fill their hand

source.ref: Morehead, A. H. and Mott-Smith, G. (eds) (1983). Hoyle's rules of games: descriptions of indoor games of skill and chance, with advice on skillful play. 2nd revised edition. New York: Signet. ISBN 978-0-451-16309-7.

pairs.tendency: A race to touch the same card needs a rule for whose hand was first, or every round turns into an argument.
pros: Quick hands matter more than planning
Anyone can win a round
cons: Several hands land at once
Rules about the lowest hand, or the turning hand, have to settle ties

source.ref: Morehead, A. H. and Mott-Smith, G. (eds) (1983). Hoyle's rules of games: descriptions of indoor games of skill and chance, with advice on skillful play. 2nd revised edition. New York: Signet. ISBN 978-0-451-16309-7.

pairs.tendency: When the shuffle decides everything, a game to win every card can run very long, and some groups never name a winner.
pros: Nothing to learn before playing
Children and adults play on equal terms
cons: No turn holds a real decision
The game can go on for a very long time

source.ref: Morehead, A. H. and Mott-Smith, G. (eds) (1983). Hoyle's rules of games: descriptions of indoor games of skill and chance, with advice on skillful play. 2nd revised edition. New York: Signet. ISBN 978-0-451-16309-7.

pairs.tendency: In Mill, a row of three lets you remove an enemy piece, so building and attacking are one move.
pros: One move builds and attacks together
Opening and closing a row can score again and again
cons: Forcing a row too early can leave your pieces locked in
Pieces already in a row cannot be taken

source.ref: Morehead, A. H. and Mott-Smith, G. (eds) (1983). Hoyle's rules of games: descriptions of indoor games of skill and chance, with advice on skillful play. 2nd revised edition. New York: Signet. ISBN 978-0-451-16309-7.

pairs.tendency: Asking for a card tells everyone you hold one of that rank, so each question gives away a little.
pros: Questions carry clues about other hands
Remembering past questions helps
cons: Every ask shows part of your own hand
A player who forgets the asks falls behind

source.ref: Morehead, A. H. and Mott-Smith, G. (eds) (1983). Hoyle's rules of games: descriptions of indoor games of skill and chance, with advice on skillful play. 2nd revised edition. New York: Signet. ISBN 978-0-451-16309-7.

pairs.tendency: A scorepad where each box is used once lets players put a low throw into a cheap box.
pros: Re-rolls soften a low throw
A spare box absorbs a failed try
cons: Each box is spent for the rest of the game
Late in the game few boxes are left to use

source.ref: Morehead, A. H. and Mott-Smith, G. (eds) (1983). Hoyle's rules of games: descriptions of indoor games of skill and chance, with advice on skillful play. 2nd revised edition. New York: Signet. ISBN 978-0-451-16309-7.

pairs.tendency: When hits are told but not which shot made them, players have to work out where the ships lie while their own fleet shrinks.
pros: Only counts of hits are told
Each sunk ship cuts the shots left
cons: Losing ships also shrinks your own attack
A lucky salvo can reveal a whole layout

source.ref: Morehead, A. H. and Mott-Smith, G. (eds) (1983). Hoyle's rules of games: descriptions of indoor games of skill and chance, with advice on skillful play. 2nd revised edition. New York: Signet. ISBN 978-0-451-16309-7.

pairs.tendency: When points fall with every question asked, careful questions pay and wild guesses cost something.
pros: Each question has a price
Halving the choices is rewarded
cons: A subject nobody guesses scores only five for the answerer
Players may hold back guesses to save points

source.ref: Morehead, A. H. and Mott-Smith, G. (eds) (1983). Hoyle's rules of games: descriptions of indoor games of skill and chance, with advice on skillful play. 2nd revised edition. New York: Signet. ISBN 978-0-451-16309-7.

pairs.tendency: In a search where the only help is hot or cold, those who know can only say how near the seeker is.
pros: Everyone takes a turn as seeker
Hints tell more as the seeker nears
cons: The hint givers give away more as the seeker gets close
There is no result to compare afterwards

source.ref: Morehead, A. H. and Mott-Smith, G. (eds) (1983). Hoyle's rules of games: descriptions of indoor games of skill and chance, with advice on skillful play. 2nd revised edition. New York: Signet. ISBN 978-0-451-16309-7.

pairs.tendency: Seekers who spot the object sit down quietly and pretend to keep looking, so silence hides what you know.
pros: Sitting down says nothing aloud
Pretending to search hides your find
cons: A fixed stare gives you away
The last seeker is left looking alone

source.ref: Morehead, A. H. and Mott-Smith, G. (eds) (1983). Hoyle's rules of games: descriptions of indoor games of skill and chance, with advice on skillful play. 2nd revised edition. New York: Signet. ISBN 978-0-451-16309-7.

pairs.tendency: Everyone writes the same called letters in their own grid, so different layouts and scores come from the same calls.
pros: One shared call gives each player a private puzzle
Players can compare grids afterwards
cons: Each caller helps rivals as much as themselves
There is nothing to do to another player's grid

source.ref: Morehead, A. H. and Mott-Smith, G. (eds) (1983). Hoyle's rules of games: descriptions of indoor games of skill and chance, with advice on skillful play. 2nd revised edition. New York: Signet. ISBN 978-0-451-16309-7.

pairs.tendency: Passing cards round at once while everyone watches for a signal means the last to notice is the Pig, whatever the cards were.
pros: Nobody is knocked out before the end
Everyone has to stay alert
cons: The loser is picked by slow attention, not by the cards
A forfeit can feel heavy to a young player

source.ref: Morehead, A. H. and Mott-Smith, G. (eds) (1983). Hoyle's rules of games: descriptions of indoor games of skill and chance, with advice on skillful play. 2nd revised edition. New York: Signet. ISBN 978-0-451-16309-7.

pairs.tendency: Cards stay face down until turned, so memory of past turns decides who finds the pairs.
pros: Every turned card is seen by all
Memory becomes the skill
cons: A turn that finds nothing still helps the next player
A player who looks away loses track

source.ref: Morehead, A. H. and Mott-Smith, G. (eds) (1983). Hoyle's rules of games: descriptions of indoor games of skill and chance, with advice on skillful play. 2nd revised edition. New York: Signet. ISBN 978-0-451-16309-7.

pairs.tendency: Where early turns grab scarce prizes, players can bid for a place in the turn order, so the order itself becomes something to value.
pros: Players who think the first turn is worth most can pay for it
Late players are not left with leftovers by the luck of a roll
cons: Money spent on the order is not available for the game itself
A minimum raise is needed to stop the bidding dragging on

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: When a roll lands you on an unowned place and all may bid for it, dice pick the place but players set the price.
pros: Everyone stays involved on every turn, as a possible buyer
Players learn to judge what a place is worth to each rival
cons: Early bids tend to run too high and leave players short of cash
The first few games run slowly while players learn the prices

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: In a quiz game checked against a card, letting a rival call your answer wrong gives players a way to act against each other.
pros: A quiz of one person answering alone gains a reason to watch rivals
A wrong challenge costs the challenger, so calling it is a risk
cons: Ties between two challengers need a rule
A challenge costs nothing to a player with no prize to lose, so the rules set a cost

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: Every extra letter doubles a word's points and words found by two players score nothing, so one long word can outweigh many short ones.
pros: A player far behind can still catch up late
Players search for rare long words instead of copying common short ones
cons: Writing many short words stops paying
A board with a common word ending can decide the game

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: When each player may give one false answer all game, no answer is fully trusted, so players check new clues against old ones.
pros: Players learn to cross-check clues
The lie can be saved for the moment it hurts most
cons: One false answer can send a guesser the wrong way for many turns
A second lie needs a lot of time and scratch paper

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: Each guess also tells the rival how many letters it shares with your secret word, so a guess gives away information as well as gathering it.
pros: Players pick guesses that learn a lot and give away little
Each turn asks for two things to be worked out
cons: Learning and hiding work against each other, which can slow play
A second hidden word has to be kept and tracked

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: When the code-maker may change the secret code as long as earlier answers stay true, a lucky early guess no longer wins by itself.
pros: Skill decides more of the result than luck
The code-maker can choose answers that reveal as little as possible
cons: The code-maker has to remember every earlier answer
Cracking the code takes more guesses

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: Letting any player swap a rack tile for a blank tile on the board adds luck to a game of mostly skill.
pros: Players far behind keep a way to catch up
A blank on the board stays open to every player
cons: Luck matters more in who wins
A play using all seven tiles tends to come within a few turns

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: When losing any one kind of piece loses the game, every trade is a danger and the last piece of a kind needs guarding.
pros: Threats appear in many places at once
Games tend to be short
cons: Trades that are safe in the usual game turn into losses
A player has to watch every kind of piece at once

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: Where one side is stronger, players bid the turns they promise to win in, and the lowest promise gets that side.
pros: Unequal sides can be balanced without changing how pieces move
A bid shows what each player believes about the game
cons: A first number needs a game already played
Counting turns is slow and players tend to miscount

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: When one player makes the opening move and the other picks a side, the first player has a reason to leave things level.
pros: Going first stops being a sure advantage
The opening move tests judgement about who it favours
cons: A player can prepare an opening in advance
The choosing player has to see the whole position, so hidden cards or dice break it

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: When each player holds the stronger side on one board and the weaker on another, the first win on either counts.
pros: A player is on both sides of the same fight
Neither player waits to see the rival's result first
cons: Two sets of equipment are needed
The player who moved first has a one-move lead unless a rule evens it

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: When two boards are played side by side and both players use each roll, one on each board, both get the same luck, though luck still plays a part.
pros: Neither player gets luckier dice over the whole game
The result shows who used each roll more cleverly
cons: A roll can still suit one board more than the other
Two boards are needed, and players may copy each other unless a screen is used

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: Every player gets the same letters and plays on their own sheet at the same time, so nobody can block anybody.
pros: No one waits for a turn
Nobody can take a spot you were saving
cons: Players never affect each other's boards
Scores are only compared at the end

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: When a turn means choosing which of several boards to move on, each turn goes to the board where a move counts most.
pros: Each move has a cost, because the other boards wait
Players judge which game is closest to being decided
cons: Giving a rival two or three moves in a row on one board can cost the others
Mixed games need rules for special cases

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: When players roll first and then pick which board to use the roll on, the dice are still random, but the player chooses where each roll goes.
pros: The choice softens a roll that would be awkward on one board
Players need to know all the boards at once
cons: Choosing the board before the roll takes the choice away
Special throws such as doubles need a rule for where the extra roll goes

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: When teammates may talk, a captain settles disagreements; when they may not, they simply alternate moves.
pros: More people than the game allows can still take part
The captain ends a stalemate between teammates
cons: Waits between turns grow with more players
A skilled player can overrule a less skilled teammate unless skills match

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: In a three-player game with no hidden cards and no dice, the leader is attacked by the other two, so leading is a danger.
pros: Alliances change as the leader changes
One player against a team of two avoids the problem
cons: A losing player may have to choose which rival wins
Players tend to look behind on purpose, which turns the game into talk

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: In three-handed hearts the player with one extra card has a large edge, which evens out only if each player gets it equally often.
pros: Each player gets the extra card in turn
Shooting the moon is a real threat
cons: The number of deals has to divide by three
One or two players can stay behind for a whole session

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: The scores of all players always add up to zero, so players join up for a hand to stop someone scoring too much.
pros: Alliances form and break within one hand
A runaway score is checked by the others
cons: Players need a score chart to follow what each result is worth
A hand where everyone takes some points is thrown in and does not count

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: When a hand gains value if it never came up and loses value if it came most, hands come to score alike.
pros: Rare hands become worth chasing
No single hand dominates
cons: Players keep a record of which hands scored
Values change between sessions, so players recall which numbers apply

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: If a defender may retreat and the attacker loses one army for it, the defender need not fight unlucky dice to the end.
pros: Defenders have a choice besides rolling
Attackers need at least three armies to attack safely
cons: Attacks cost more than before
A player cannot leave a place empty, which limits the choice

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: When a place is struck by an accident, its armies vanish and later armies entering it are halved, so the damage stays all game.
pros: Players avoid piling armies into one place
The map looks different as the game goes on
cons: Marked places no longer count towards holding a continent
A player who holds a key place can lose it by luck

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: Both players write their moves down and reveal them together, then fight where armies meet, so each guesses where the rival will go.
pros: Nobody waits for the other's move
A move that gathers armies and a move that spreads them can beat each other
cons: Moves are written and checked, so that nobody argues
The smaller force is wiped out, so a wrong guess costs heavily

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: In five-in-a-row games where a pair can be captured by being sandwiched, building a line also exposes it to attack.
pros: A player can win by building or by capturing
Extending a threatened pair into a line of three escapes the capture
cons: A stone is only safe between rival stones if you place it there yourself
Letting lines of three be captured raises the captures needed

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: In duplicate bridge, a made contract scores nothing if rivals take more tricks, so players risk the contract for one more.
pros: The same hand is played differently under different scoring
Extra tricks count as well as making the contract
cons: A player may fail a contract trying for more
Players need to know which scoring form is in use before bidding

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: When the side with fewer high cards gets a bonus from a table, the luck of the deal counts for less, though it still counts.
pros: Players with a thin hand still earn something
The bonus is read from a table, so nobody's opinion decides it
cons: Played cards are kept in front of players so high cards can be counted
The table is looked up after every deal

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: In stud poker, when a player can pay to pass a face-up card on, players shape each other's hands and pots grow large.
pros: Players can collect very high or very low hands
Passing a card is itself a signal to rivals
cons: Players tend to fold less, so pots grow
A card passed to a rival who then holds a big hand can hurt the passer

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: Where moving first is a large edge, giving the second player extra points evens the game, and a half point avoids ties.
pros: The edge of going first can be priced in points
A half point stops a tied score
cons: The right number is disputed, even among top players
Different players still prefer to go first or second

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: In a game of holding space, a smaller board plays faster and suits beginners, while a larger board gives more room for skill.
pros: Beginners can learn the game in less time
Experts can keep finding new ideas on a larger board
cons: A very small board shows little of the game
A very large board takes much longer

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: With extra suits in a card game, hands hold shorter suits and more empty suits, so declarers can make plays not possible before.
pros: New plays such as passing a trick between hands become available
Players meet unfamiliar situations that leave experts and beginners alike unsure
cons: Players agree in advance how new suits rank and score
Marking extra cards by hand takes effort

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: When nothing is hidden and luck plays no part, a gap in skill shows in every move, so players add a head start.
pros: The less skilled player keeps a real chance of winning
Both players learn more from a close game
cons: The head start has to be tuned over many games
Someone has to keep track of it

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: Letting the less skilled player take back his last move once per turn is a handicap that adds no equipment.
pros: The game itself stays the same
The less skilled player can try a plan and undo it
cons: A second move you regret in the same turn cannot be undone
The more skilled player's reply can be wasted

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: Removing a piece from the more skilled side lets the other side trade down; where captured pieces return, a head start costs less.
pros: A head start can be given without changing the game
Pieces that return keep trades from simplifying the board
cons: Taking a piece away can push play towards trades
Each game needs its own head-start rules

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: When each player makes two moves in a turn in a game about holding space, a group needs more room to stay safe.
pros: Fights go differently from the usual game
The same board and stones are used
cons: Habits from the usual game stop working
An attacker gets two moves before the other player can reply

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: Putting down several joined pieces in one turn makes a space-holding game shorter and changes how fights start.
pros: The game takes less time
Choosing a shape becomes part of the plan
cons: Players have to learn which shapes are allowed
The first player needs a limit on the first turn to stay level

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: If a game ends at the first capture and nobody may pass, sacrificing stones to gain time stops working.
pros: Games end with a sudden finish
Stones are not captured until the end, so paper and coloured pencils will do
cons: Late moves are forced into your own space
One careless move ends the whole game

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: Changing the grid changes how easily stones are captured: on a hexagon grid six stones are needed instead of four.
pros: A grid can be redrawn on paper for free
A regular grid lets players carry what they learn to every part of the board
cons: Groups are hard to capture, so extra rules may be needed
Players have to relearn their tactics

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: A group that holds a ring of six points cannot be captured, which gives players a shape to aim for.
pros: Survival becomes easier on a grid where two safe spaces are hard to make
A ring gives a plain goal in the opening
cons: Where pieces can move, breaking the ring ends the safety
Players have to learn the ring rule before play

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: In a race to fill the far corner, a piece left behind in that corner can stop the other player from ever finishing.
pros: A player can slow a leader without attacking
The board gets crowded as both sides arrive
cons: A rule is needed so one piece cannot stall the game for ever
Players may spend turns blocking instead of racing

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: When a piece on the far row wins unless it is captured at once, every move is both an advance and a threat.
pros: Attack and defence are tied to the same pieces
The game can end suddenly
cons: A player who copies the other in mirror image can force a draw, so an extra rule is needed
Players have to watch the whole board every turn

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: In a pure race, the player who moves first is a step ahead, and the other can only draw by arriving straight after.
pros: The aim is easy to see
One late arrival can still save a draw
cons: The first mover has a built-in edge
Opening moves tend to repeat

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: When both players use the same stones to carry the ball home, a chain built for you also serves the other player.
pros: Delaying a jump to build a longer chain is a real plan
Jumped stones are removed, so a used chain is gone
cons: A chain can help the other player as much as you
Stones left a knight's move from the ball tend to be of little use

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: In a race to line up five stones, the first player has an edge, so limits are put on his early moves.
pros: The rules are very short
Limits on the first player keep the sides close
cons: The first player still has an edge at the start
Extra limits add many rules to learn

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: A board that wraps round like a doughnut has no centre and no edge, so the first move has no favoured place.
pros: Lines can run off one edge and return on the other
Every starting point is alike
cons: Players find it hard to picture a line that leaves one edge and comes back
A flat sheet of paper needs a rule for the wrap

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: When any of several shapes wins, one stone can threaten more than one, and a threat to close a ring gains time.
pros: Many ways to threaten, with one simple rule
Draws are very rare
cons: A ring is almost never completed, so it works mostly as a threat
Three winning shapes are more to learn than one

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: Scoring each word at double the one before it, 10, 20, then 40, makes one long word worth as much as several short ones.
pros: Players work for longer words
Overlapping words score separately
cons: Only the longer word counts when one word sits inside another
A score table is needed

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: When every player writes the same called letters into a hidden grid, everyone builds with the same pieces but ends with a different pattern.
pros: Little equipment is needed
Each player's grid is their own plan
cons: Nobody sees how others did until the end
More players means less room for strategy

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: Winning by capturing a run of numbered pieces, such as 4-5-6-7-8, makes players choose which pieces to take, not only how many.
pros: Each capture matters differently
Players watch which numbers the other holds
cons: Players have to track the numbers taken and left
Taking any piece is not enough to win

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: Anyone may call a word the moment they see it and others may steal it, so no word is safe.
pros: Nobody waits for a turn
Stolen words keep the table busy
cons: Slower readers may get few words
Players need to agree in advance which words count

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: When every move has to flip at least one piece, taking fewer pieces early tends to leave the other player with fewer moves.
pros: Holding back leaves the other player short of choices
Key squares such as corners fall late in the game
cons: Taking many pieces early tends to give the other player more moves
Players are drawn to the move that takes the most pieces

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: If captured pieces change colour instead of leaving the board, a lead can turn round in a single move.
pros: Pieces never run out
A player who is behind can come back in one move
cons: A wall of pieces can look safe and still be open to a recapture
Players have to check every piece in the wall

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: When a player can still take points already stored away, a lead is not final until the game ends.
pros: The result stays open to the end
A player who is behind keeps a chance
cons: Points kept in a store are never completely safe
A player cannot count on a lead

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: When the player sowing beads may choose which bead goes into which pit, the moves per turn rise from a handful to hundreds.
pros: The order of sowing matters
Luck plays no part
cons: A player has far more moves to weigh each turn
Beads of several values have to be kept straight

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: Moving a marker along a track instead of placing a stone turns a pass into points and evens out the first move.
pros: A pass has a price
The first-move edge can be adjusted by where the marker starts
cons: A separate track has to be drawn
Players have to learn to add the marker points

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: With fewer shelters than pieces, players race to fill them and can shut each other out, and the one left outside loses.
pros: Only one piece has to find a place
Filling a shelter can block another player
cons: One slow piece decides the whole game
A large board and many pieces take a long time

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: If both teams can score in the same game, players play a series until one side reaches an agreed total.
pros: A lost piece does not end everything
There are several ways to score
cons: A series takes more time
Players have to keep a running tally

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: When dice only say which kind of piece may move, and a player may use one die, both or neither, luck limits choices.
pros: Allies may talk over the roll
A player can skip a roll that does not help
cons: A lucky double can hurt the other side heavily
Four players take a long time over one game

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: Without dice, allied armies play pure strategy, and the order in which allies and rivals move matters as much as each piece.
pros: Every move comes from a player's choice
Allies can plan together
cons: Players have to keep track of the turn order
A mistake in order cannot be blamed on a roll

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: The dealer knows the secret rule and, once play begins, may only say right or wrong, so everyone gets the same plain answers.
pros: The dealer cannot steer play
The rule is written down to be checked afterwards
cons: One player sits out each round as dealer
A rule that is too hard may teach the others nothing

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: Players test guesses about a hidden rule by seeing which plays are accepted, much as scientists test guesses about nature.
pros: Every play gives the whole table a clue
A wrong play still gives information
cons: A wrong play costs cards
Beginners tend to set a rule harder than they think

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: When the dealer's score depends on the others' scores, a secret rule neither too easy nor too hard pays the dealer most.
pros: The dealer has a reason to set a fair puzzle
Players keep guessing instead of giving up
cons: Scoring takes several steps to work out
A rule that lets half the cards be played is harder to find than one that lets a quarter be played

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: In charades with bidding, players bid how few minutes and seconds they need to get a teammate to name the phrase.
pros: A bid turns a vague boast into a number
The clock gives a clear pass or fail
cons: A bold bid that runs out of time loses the team a point
The game needs a trustworthy timer

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: The team of the lowest bidder earns a point if a teammate names the phrase within the bid, and loses a point if not.
pros: Teammates share the reward for a quick guess
The bidder only has to judge their own team's skill
cons: One player's boast can cost every teammate a point
Each team needs a bidder who can judge how hard a phrase is

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: Before bidding, one player from each team sees the secret phrase. They then bid on how fast they could act it out.
pros: Bidders bid with the answer in front of them
Both bidders see the same phrase, so bids compare judgement
cons: The actor can only mime, so a low bid is hard to keep
A low bid tells rival bidders the phrase looks easy

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: In Haggle each player gets a sealed envelope of twelve cards and trades with anyone, for cards or for information.
pros: Deals can be made any way: card for card, information for information
Nobody can tell which suit to chase
cons: A trade partner may hide what a card is really worth
A player judges every deal knowing only part of what the others hold

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: In Haggle each scoring rule sits on a secret sheet, so players piece together how cards score by trading sheets.
pros: Trading information matters as much as trading cards
Two sheets read together tell more than either alone
cons: The host has to write rules that do not contradict one another
A player may trade away a sheet that was worth a lot

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: In Haggle all trading ends before the host scores each envelope, so nobody knows the totals until the end.
pros: Trading stays busy because nobody knows who is ahead
The final choice of which cards to hand in decides the result
cons: The host needs time to score every envelope by hand
A player cannot check their own score while dealing

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: In Haggle the first twelve cards are dealt by chance, but trading lets a player swap away cards they do not want.
pros: Trading softens a first hand with little use
Caps on the highest cards stop a lucky deal from deciding the winner
cons: Players who are dealt useful information sheets still start ahead
The host has to design the caps with care

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: In Super Babel players trade cards one for one to build two five-card poker hands, or one special ten-card hand.
pros: Equal trades keep every hand at ten cards
Players can call out what they need or keep their hands secret, and alliances can form
cons: A scorekeeper has to record every hand and reshuffle
Players need a time limit agreed beforehand

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: Super Babel has no turns. Everyone trades at once until a set time, such as twenty minutes, ends the game.
pros: Players bargain whenever they like
A player who goes out gets a new packet and rejoins at once
cons: The game is made for fifteen or more players, so small groups have few partners
A non-playing scorekeeper is needed

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: A doubling cube lets a player double the stakes of a dice game. The other accepts, or gives up the game.
pros: Judging your own winning chances becomes a skill that decides a series
The same cube suits other race games, such as Parcheesi
cons: Judging the odds is hard, and the score of a match changes the choice
Refusing a double loses the game at once

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: In Moultezim and Gioul pieces cannot hit a single enemy piece, and in Plakato a hit piece is pinned instead of sent off.
pros: Progress is never sent back to the start
Players block each other by where pieces stand
cons: A pinned piece cannot move until the hitting piece moves away
Players lose the sudden swing of sending a piece home

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: In Dice Chess a die decides which kind of piece may move, but every piece stays in view.
pros: Rolls make memorised openings less useful
Players can still plan with the whole board in sight
cons: A roll may leave only one piece able to move
A roll for a missing or blocked piece is thrown again

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: In Refusal Chess a player may reject the opponent's move, and in Compromise Chess the opponent picks one of two offered moves.
pros: Each choice carries a guess about the opponent's reply
Tactics and psychology both matter
cons: Players slow down to weigh what to offer
A single legal move cannot be refused

pairs.tendency: In Crash each player guesses a hidden five-letter word, and the other reports how many letters sit in the right place.
pros: Every reply is a clue that narrows the next guess
The game needs only paper and a dictionary, so letters can carry it
cons: A wrong score from the replier loses the game
Both players need to agree on a dictionary first

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: Double Move Chess gives each player two moves a turn and drops check, so games tend to end quickly.
pros: Short games finish in fewer letters
Each letter carries two moves
cons: Check and checkmate are dropped, so the king needs watching on every move
Moving into check is allowed, which changes habits learned from ordinary chess

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: In map-colouring games players colour one region a turn, and the first player with no legal region to colour loses.
pros: Players block each other only through the colours already placed
Extra colours make the game harder to work out
cons: Giving each player their own colour makes it harder still
Touching regions can end the game suddenly

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: In Finger Baseball both players show one to five fingers at the same moment, and a match gives the batter a hit.
pros: The game needs no equipment beyond one hand
Hidden choices stop a fixed habit from working for long
cons: An observant opponent can use any pattern in your choices
No single choice wins every time

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: In Ghost each player adds a letter. A rival may challenge a letter they think leads to no word, and the speaker then names a word.
pros: A bluff is tested at once by the challenge
The game needs no equipment
cons: A wrong challenge costs the challenger a letter
Adding letters at either end, as in Super Ghost, makes the possibilities very hard to count

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: In Kickball Golf each player kicks a ball at a tree or can, hole by hole, against a fixed par.
pros: One player can play alone against par
Each round takes only a few minutes
cons: A ball in the way needs marking with a leaf or twig
Kicking needs open ground clear of windows and children

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: In Poison croquet a ball that finishes the course turns poison. It knocks out any ball it hits.
pros: Finishing does not end the game for the finisher
Finished players stay in the game and threaten others
cons: A poison ball that hits the stake is out
Knocked-out players wait while the game goes on

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: In Nim a counting rule shows the mover which objects to take, so a player who knows it wins from many positions.
pros: The rules and equipment are very simple
Adding a second dimension of rows and columns makes the game hard again
cons: Once the rule is known, winning becomes routine
Two equal sections let the second player copy every move

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: When each player gets a few re-throws, or coins to nudge a roll up or down by one, an unwanted roll can be answered.
pros: A player can plan when to spend a re-throw.
One unwanted roll need not decide a whole turn.
cons: Players have to keep count of what they have left.
Spending early leaves nothing for a turn that matters more.

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: With a list of all 36 rolls to cross off, and no reuse until the list ends, luck drops out of the dice.
pros: Winning depends on the order in which rolls are used.
Nobody wins by throwing more double sixes.
cons: The game stops feeling like a dice game.
Each player keeps a list and crosses off rolls.

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: With the list of unused rolls open, the chance of any roll is either certain or none, and both players can see which.
pros: Each player can see which rolls the other has left.
Counting replaces guessing at odds.
cons: Using up every roll that holds one number gives the other player a fixed target.
Players have to look at the list before each move.

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: In a game by post, players can take the next dice roll from a public number they agree on, such as a temperature.
pros: Both players can check each roll against the same published number.
No third person is needed to throw the dice.
cons: The source of numbers has to be agreed before play.
Each roll waits until the number is published.

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: In a game by post, each move goes on a card or letter, written in a short, clear notation.
pros: Players can think as long as they like about a move.
People who live far apart can play.
cons: A game can take weeks.
The two players need an agreed way of writing moves.

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: Giving one player more re-throws than the other can offset the edge of going first.
pros: The edge of moving first can be reduced by a small gift.
Players can choose the size of the gift.
cons: The two players need to agree the numbers first.
A player with fewer re-throws has less to fall back on after an unwanted roll.

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: If players throw three dice and choose which two to use, each throw still leaves room for a choice.
pros: Players decide which numbers to keep.
An unwanted throw is less likely to ruin a turn.
cons: There is more to look at on every turn.
Moves become less of a surprise.

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: In a game of pure skill, if sitting back and waiting is the winning plan, both players wait for the other to weaken.
pros: A reward for attacking, such as a promotion, gives players a reason to move forward.
More mobile pieces give attackers more ways in.
cons: Games can run long and may never end.
A player who attacks can open weaknesses in their own position.

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: Giving each player two moves a turn instead of one can raise a player's attacking power and shorten the game.
pros: Attacks come faster.
The game can end sooner.
cons: The other player waits through two moves before replying.
A plan can be finished before the other player can answer.

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: If a game seems to favour one side, players can bid for the right to go first.
pros: The player who values going first most pays for it.
Both players start with a say in who moves first.
cons: The game gains a step before the first move.
Players need some way to measure what going first is worth.

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: If no player may recreate an earlier board position, players have to vary their moves instead of repeating them.
pros: Fewer games end in a draw by repeating moves.
A player who is blocked can make a threat elsewhere first, then come back.
cons: Players have to remember or record earlier positions.
A fight over one spot can last many turns, until one player runs out of threats.

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: In a Refusal game, the other player may reject a move, and the mover then has to make a different one.
pros: The other player shapes which moves are played.
A mover has to think about what the other will accept.
cons: A player can be pushed into a move they did not first choose.
Each turn takes longer.

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: In a Compromise game, a player proposes two moves each turn and the other player picks which one is played.
pros: The other player has a hand in every move.
A mover has to offer two moves they can live with.
cons: Each turn needs two usable ideas instead of one.
The strongest move may never be on the table.

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: In Open Scrabble, all tiles lie face up in one line and players draw only from its two ends.
pros: Each player can see exactly what the other can take.
Luck leaves the tile draw.
cons: Working out what the other will be able to take is very hard.
Racks have to stay in view all game.

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: In Double Bughouse, two teams play on two boards with a clock each, and a piece one partner captures goes to the other.
pros: Partners can talk and ask each other for a piece.
A team can win when an opponent's clock runs out.
cons: A player in trouble may stop moving and let the clock run, hoping a partner wins first.
Play gets noisy and rushed.

pairs.tendency: Where your hands decide the shot, an attack can mean landing on top of an opponent's piece to trap it.
pros: Attacking needs no cards, dice or hidden plans
A single clever shot can freeze a rival piece
cons: Every attack rests on a shot nobody can repeat exactly
A trapped piece can sit out many turns

pairs.tendency: When players shoot from where the last shot stopped, a short shot hands the other player an easy first shot.
pros: Each shot changes the next player's position
Every shot carries risk without any extra rule

Players cannot attack directly, only leave things in a spot

pairs.tendency: In a steady-hand game, a turn tends to run until the first slip, then passes on.
pros: Players are watching closely while the others try
A clean run lets one player keep going
cons: A slip ends the turn at once, however it began
Waiting players have little to do but watch
