pairs.tendency: A dexterity game can count what was taken or landed, so one steady turn adds many points.
pros: A tally is easy to keep and to check
Different objects can be worth different amounts
cons: A long run can leave others far behind
A single slip early on can cost a whole turn's worth

source.ref: Spadaccini, S. (2005). The big book of rules: board games, kids' games, card games, from backgammon and bocce to tiddlywinks and stickball. New York: Plume. ISBN 978-0-452-28644-3.

pairs.tendency: When two dice are rolled and each number moves a piece, the dice set the distance but you choose which piece moves.
pros: Players keep a real choice on every turn
A low roll can still be used with some care
cons: Careful play cannot make up for a long run of low rolls
Players have to work out many options on each roll

source.ref: Spadaccini, S. (2005). The big book of rules: board games, kids' games, card games, from backgammon and bocce to tiddlywinks and stickball. New York: Plume. ISBN 978-0-452-28644-3.

pairs.tendency: A dice race can carry a doubling die, so a player can ask for twice the stakes during the game.
pros: The other player has to accept or give up on the spot
Stakes can grow without limit as the game goes on
cons: A player who is behind may be pressed to give up early
Playing for money changes why people sit down to play

source.ref: Spadaccini, S. (2005). The big book of rules: board games, kids' games, card games, from backgammon and bocce to tiddlywinks and stickball. New York: Plume. ISBN 978-0-452-28644-3.

pairs.tendency: When players hold tiles that others cannot see, each move also tells the others something about what is held.
pros: Players keep some of their plans private
A tile not played says something about the hand
cons: A very lucky draw can decide a round
Players who watch closely may work out your hand

source.ref: Spadaccini, S. (2005). The big book of rules: board games, kids' games, card games, from backgammon and bocce to tiddlywinks and stickball. New York: Plume. ISBN 978-0-452-28644-3.

pairs.tendency: In a game where players keep their tiles out of sight, the tiles an opponent does not play can show what the hand holds.
pros: Careful watching is rewarded
Counting played tiles gives a clue to the rest
cons: Keeping count asks for steady attention
Beginners may not know where to start

source.ref: Spadaccini, S. (2005). The big book of rules: board games, kids' games, card games, from backgammon and bocce to tiddlywinks and stickball. New York: Plume. ISBN 978-0-452-28644-3.

pairs.tendency: A line of tiles grows from two ends, so a score can come from the numbers that sit at the ends.
pros: Players aim for a total as well as for getting rid of tiles
The line changes the options for the next player
cons: Players may leave a score open for the next player
Totals reward arithmetic more than tile skills

source.ref: Spadaccini, S. (2005). The big book of rules: board games, kids' games, card games, from backgammon and bocce to tiddlywinks and stickball. New York: Plume. ISBN 978-0-452-28644-3.

pairs.tendency: The draw of tiles brings luck, and the skill is in choosing where to place each one.
pros: Drawing more tiles can add variety to a hand
A player can plan the use of the heaviest tiles
cons: The draw can leave a hand with no tile that fits
Heavy tiles stuck in hand cost points

source.ref: Spadaccini, S. (2005). The big book of rules: board games, kids' games, card games, from backgammon and bocce to tiddlywinks and stickball. New York: Plume. ISBN 978-0-452-28644-3.

pairs.tendency: A hand of tiles is spent over many turns, so players choose which to play first and which to keep.
pros: Holding varied tiles gives more options later
Players can keep a number for both ends of the line
cons: Heavy tiles left late can be costly
Drawing to find a play can swell the hand

source.ref: Spadaccini, S. (2005). The big book of rules: board games, kids' games, card games, from backgammon and bocce to tiddlywinks and stickball. New York: Plume. ISBN 978-0-452-28644-3.

pairs.tendency: When each player has to answer the one before, a slip puts the player out and the circle shrinks.
pros: Rules are simple to teach
Everyone is listening to the last answer
cons: Players who go out early wait through the rest
One slip can end a long run of right answers

source.ref: Spadaccini, S. (2005). The big book of rules: board games, kids' games, card games, from backgammon and bocce to tiddlywinks and stickball. New York: Plume. ISBN 978-0-452-28644-3.

pairs.tendency: In a word-building chain, a player can challenge the one before and ask them to name a word.
pros: A bluff can be tested at once
A dictionary settles a challenge, so nobody argues
cons: A wrong challenge costs the challenger
Players may hold back for fear of being challenged

source.ref: Spadaccini, S. (2005). The big book of rules: board games, kids' games, card games, from backgammon and bocce to tiddlywinks and stickball. New York: Plume. ISBN 978-0-452-28644-3.

pairs.tendency: A chain of replies can have one goal for the whole group, such as finishing the alphabet in time.
pros: Players listen and build on each other's lines
Each sentence helps the next speaker
cons: One stuck player can cost the whole group
A tight rule on letters can slow the scene

source.ref: Spadaccini, S. (2005). The big book of rules: board games, kids' games, card games, from backgammon and bocce to tiddlywinks and stickball. New York: Plume. ISBN 978-0-452-28644-3.

pairs.tendency: Players can build a scene together by answering each other, with nobody trying to beat anyone.
pros: Everyone shares the same aim
Laughter comes from the odd turns the scene takes
cons: Players who freeze can feel they have let the rest down
There is no single winner to decide who played the most

source.ref: Spadaccini, S. (2005). The big book of rules: board games, kids' games, card games, from backgammon and bocce to tiddlywinks and stickball. New York: Plume. ISBN 978-0-452-28644-3.

pairs.tendency: A scene that has to follow a strict rule, like starting each line with the next letter, tends to head somewhere odd.
pros: The rule gives players a reason to say unusual things
Odd turns are accepted because the rule forces them
cons: The scene can lose its thread
Not every player finds nonsense easy

source.ref: Spadaccini, S. (2005). The big book of rules: board games, kids' games, card games, from backgammon and bocce to tiddlywinks and stickball. New York: Plume. ISBN 978-0-452-28644-3.

pairs.tendency: A question-and-answer game lets one player work out a hidden fact from the replies.
pros: Each answer narrows the choices
Questions can be chosen to cut the field in half
cons: Vague questions waste turns
Answerers who give little away can slow the game

source.ref: Spadaccini, S. (2005). The big book of rules: board games, kids' games, card games, from backgammon and bocce to tiddlywinks and stickball. New York: Plume. ISBN 978-0-452-28644-3.

pairs.tendency: In a guessing round, the player who names the secret first wins the round and takes over the secret.
pros: The aim is simple to say
Roles move from player to player
cons: A quick wrong guess can waste a turn
Others may wait through a long round

source.ref: Spadaccini, S. (2005). The big book of rules: board games, kids' games, card games, from backgammon and bocce to tiddlywinks and stickball. New York: Plume. ISBN 978-0-452-28644-3.

pairs.tendency: When a team has to hide a coin without a sound, its players bluff with quiet hands and steady faces.
pros: The hiding depends on the group moving together
The other team has only bodies and the table to read
cons: Any noise gives the hiding place away
Players who laugh can give the coin away

source.ref: Spadaccini, S. (2005). The big book of rules: board games, kids' games, card games, from backgammon and bocce to tiddlywinks and stickball. New York: Plume. ISBN 978-0-452-28644-3.

pairs.tendency: A team hiding a coin moves together, and each member's quietness helps the others.
pros: Each player has a clear part to play
The team can plan how to hide the sound
cons: One noisy player can spoil it for all
The other team has little to go on but guesswork

source.ref: Spadaccini, S. (2005). The big book of rules: board games, kids' games, card games, from backgammon and bocce to tiddlywinks and stickball. New York: Plume. ISBN 978-0-452-28644-3.

pairs.tendency: In murder and Mafia games, only the secret killer may lie, so a calm face and a steady story are the main tools.
pros: Players learn to watch faces and stories
The lie has a clear owner, with no extra rule
cons: The killer carries the whole strain of lying
Honest players cannot prove they are honest

source.ref: Spadaccini, S. (2005). The big book of rules: board games, kids' games, card games, from backgammon and bocce to tiddlywinks and stickball. New York: Plume. ISBN 978-0-452-28644-3.

pairs.tendency: In Killer, victims may say only when and where they were struck, so the group has to work out the killer from where everyone was.
pros: Everyone has a clue to share
Comparing where people were gives the group something to talk about
cons: A killer who stays out of sight leaves little to compare
Players struck early may have little to add

source.ref: Spadaccini, S. (2005). The big book of rules: board games, kids' games, card games, from backgammon and bocce to tiddlywinks and stickball. New York: Plume. ISBN 978-0-452-28644-3.

pairs.tendency: When a Killer game runs for hours before a meeting, the secret has to be kept through the rest of the day as well as at a table.
pros: Suspicion builds slowly between kills
The game fits into a day that is already full
cons: Players may forget they are playing
A player who leaves early cannot be counted at the meeting

source.ref: Spadaccini, S. (2005). The big book of rules: board games, kids' games, card games, from backgammon and bocce to tiddlywinks and stickball. New York: Plume. ISBN 978-0-452-28644-3.

pairs.tendency: In Hollywood Connections, a player names a link and may be challenged to prove it, so a bluff costs a point if the challenger is right.
pros: A guess can be tried when no sure link is known
A challenge ends the chain with a fact to check
cons: A challenger who is wrong hands over the point
The game needs a book or a phone to settle arguments

source.ref: Spadaccini, S. (2005). The big book of rules: board games, kids' games, card games, from backgammon and bocce to tiddlywinks and stickball. New York: Plume. ISBN 978-0-452-28644-3.

pairs.tendency: When each player has to answer within a few seconds, anyone who stalls is out, and the chain goes on among those left.
pros: The rule is quick to say
Players stay alert as the group shrinks
cons: Players who are out wait with nothing to do
A slow thinker leaves early, whatever they know

source.ref: Spadaccini, S. (2005). The big book of rules: board games, kids' games, card games, from backgammon and bocce to tiddlywinks and stickball. New York: Plume. ISBN 978-0-452-28644-3.

pairs.tendency: In word chains, a ten-second limit turns every reply into a quick recall, so the player does not have time to plan far ahead.
pros: Replies come fast
Players hear many examples in a short time
cons: A player who knows the answer can still lose it under pressure
Easier words come up again and again

source.ref: Spadaccini, S. (2005). The big book of rules: board games, kids' games, card games, from backgammon and bocce to tiddlywinks and stickball. New York: Plume. ISBN 978-0-452-28644-3.

pairs.tendency: In Fortunately, Unfortunately, the sentences swing between lucky and unlucky news until one player is stumped, and only that player has lost.
pros: No scoring needed
The story turns in directions nobody planned
cons: The stumped player is named in front of the others
A confident group may go on for a long time

source.ref: Spadaccini, S. (2005). The big book of rules: board games, kids' games, card games, from backgammon and bocce to tiddlywinks and stickball. New York: Plume. ISBN 978-0-452-28644-3.

pairs.tendency: In Telephone, nobody wins; players pass a whispered phrase along and laugh at how it changed at the end.
pros: Nobody is left out
The change in the phrase is the whole interest
cons: Some players want a score to care about
Players near the end see mistakes they did not make

pairs.tendency: In marbles, a player who knocks a marble out of the ring keeps it and shoots again, so skill turns straight into a growing pile.
pros: A clean shot pays at once
The count of marbles is easy to check

A lucky opening shot can decide much of the game

A miss costs only the turn, not the ground gained

A cap in the middle zone can sit stuck until someone hits it

pros: One shot does two jobs
Attacks need no cards or dice

Players behind in the game can still change the result with one hit

pros: Everyone else is safe
A missed throw has a clear cost

A player with three letters may play more carefully than the rest

The jail gives caught players a way back

A team that guards too much may never cross the line

pros: A game with no capture still has a result
Teams that guard well still gain
cons: A team may chase prisoners and forget the flag
The count of prisoners is easy to dispute

source.ref: Spadaccini, S. (2005). The big book of rules: board games, kids' games, card games, from backgammon and bocce to tiddlywinks and stickball. New York: Plume. ISBN 978-0-452-28644-3.

pairs.tendency: In Shout It Out, one team shouts its words together, so the other team has to pick one phrase out of a jumble of voices.
pros: Everyone on a team takes part at once
The score falls for each extra shout
cons: A loud player can drown out the quiet ones
The guessing team may hear only noise

source.ref: Spadaccini, S. (2005). The big book of rules: board games, kids' games, card games, from backgammon and bocce to tiddlywinks and stickball. New York: Plume. ISBN 978-0-452-28644-3.

pairs.tendency: In charades, each actor has two minutes and the total time counts, so a clear first gesture saves the whole team time.
pros: Every turn gets the same time
A set of signs speeds things up
cons: New players may not know the signs
A hard idea can use the full time with no result

source.ref: Spadaccini, S. (2005). The big book of rules: board games, kids' games, card games, from backgammon and bocce to tiddlywinks and stickball. New York: Plume. ISBN 978-0-452-28644-3.

pairs.tendency: In Western Union, a squeeze passed hand to hand has to reach one player before the player in the middle sees it.
pros: Players trust each other's hands
The signal is hard to spot
cons: The player in the middle waits with eyes shut
The direction can change, so players have to stay alert

source.ref: Spadaccini, S. (2005). The big book of rules: board games, kids' games, card games, from backgammon and bocce to tiddlywinks and stickball. New York: Plume. ISBN 978-0-452-28644-3.

pairs.tendency: In the button hunt, the hider may only say warmer or colder, so each search step brings back one small clue.
pros: The clue is simple to give
The hider has a say in how long the hunt lasts
cons: The hider has to stay quiet about where the button is
Seekers who wander far get less help at first

source.ref: Spadaccini, S. (2005). The big book of rules: board games, kids' games, card games, from backgammon and bocce to tiddlywinks and stickball. New York: Plume. ISBN 978-0-452-28644-3.

pairs.tendency: In Beetle and Bingo, each player draws or marks alone and nobody can slow another down, so the game is a race against luck.
pros: Rules are simple enough for young players
Nobody is attacked
cons: A player behind has nothing to do about it
Skill has no place to show

source.ref: Spadaccini, S. (2005). The big book of rules: board games, kids' games, card games, from backgammon and bocce to tiddlywinks and stickball. New York: Plume. ISBN 978-0-452-28644-3.

pairs.tendency: In a scavenger hunt, both teams get the same list and the first to bring everything back wins, so teams split up the list or search together.
pros: Every team member can help
A shared list makes the teams comparable
cons: A team that splits up may miss an item
A team that returns late can be ruled out

source.ref: Spadaccini, S. (2005). The big book of rules: board games, kids' games, card games, from backgammon and bocce to tiddlywinks and stickball. New York: Plume. ISBN 978-0-452-28644-3.

pairs.tendency: In Hot Potato, the player in the middle calls "hot" at a moment nobody can predict, so whoever holds the potato then is out, whatever they did.
pros: The rules take a minute to teach
Everyone stays tense until the call
cons: A player can be out through no choice of theirs
Players who are out wait for the rest

source.ref: Spadaccini, S. (2005). The big book of rules: board games, kids' games, card games, from backgammon and bocce to tiddlywinks and stickball. New York: Plume. ISBN 978-0-452-28644-3.

pairs.tendency: In Bridge, each bid is also a message from one partner to the other about the cards in a hidden hand.
pros: The bid shows a partner what you hold without showing the cards
Partners need to read each other's bids and trust them
cons: A bid can promise more than the hand holds
One partner misreading a bid can send the whole bidding off course

source.ref: Spadaccini, S. (2005). The big book of rules: board games, kids' games, card games, from backgammon and bocce to tiddlywinks and stickball. New York: Plume. ISBN 978-0-452-28644-3.

pairs.tendency: In Bridge, the bidding names how many tricks one side promises to win, and the play then tests the promise.
pros: The target is clear before the first card is played
Each round of play carries a promise to keep
cons: A high bid that fails gives points to the other side
Bidding takes time before any playing begins

source.ref: Spadaccini, S. (2005). The big book of rules: board games, kids' games, card games, from backgammon and bocce to tiddlywinks and stickball. New York: Plume. ISBN 978-0-452-28644-3.

pairs.tendency: In darts, the numbers on the board are arranged so a small miss lands on a low number.
pros: A careless throw costs points
A lucky hit is less likely to land high
cons: A beginner with a shaky aim scores low for long
Practice shows quickly in the totals

source.ref: Spadaccini, S. (2005). The big book of rules: board games, kids' games, card games, from backgammon and bocce to tiddlywinks and stickball. New York: Plume. ISBN 978-0-452-28644-3.

pairs.tendency: In Twenty-One and darts, the finish has to be exact, so a player near the end may miss on purpose.
pros: The last few points ask for steady aim as well as speed
A small lead does not settle the ending
cons: A player may have to throw badly on purpose
The ending can take many more turns than the middle

source.ref: Spadaccini, S. (2005). The big book of rules: board games, kids' games, card games, from backgammon and bocce to tiddlywinks and stickball. New York: Plume. ISBN 978-0-452-28644-3.

pairs.tendency: In Prison Dodgeball, a player who is hit waits at the side and can come back when a teammate catches a ball.
pros: Players who are out still have a way back in
The wait is shorter than in plain elimination
cons: The side with more catchers keeps bringing players back
The game can run long if both sides catch often

source.ref: Spadaccini, S. (2005). The big book of rules: board games, kids' games, card games, from backgammon and bocce to tiddlywinks and stickball. New York: Plume. ISBN 978-0-452-28644-3.

pairs.tendency: In Croquet, hitting another player's ball earns extra strokes, and sending it away costs that player ground.
pros: A player in front can be pushed back by a single hit
Hitting a rival is a way to move yourself on
cons: A turn spent on a rival's ball does not move your own ball on
Players ahead are the ones aimed at

source.ref: Spadaccini, S. (2005). The big book of rules: board games, kids' games, card games, from backgammon and bocce to tiddlywinks and stickball. New York: Plume. ISBN 978-0-452-28644-3.

pairs.tendency: In Cribbage, each player chooses which two cards to give away, knowing the rest are meant to make sums of fifteen, pairs and runs.
pros: The choice of cards to keep is the main decision
Many small patterns can score at once
cons: A hand is hard to count for a beginner
The crib gives the dealer extra points from cards both players helped pick

source.ref: Spadaccini, S. (2005). The big book of rules: board games, kids' games, card games, from backgammon and bocce to tiddlywinks and stickball. New York: Plume. ISBN 978-0-452-28644-3.

pairs.tendency: In Blackjack, the dealer keeps one card face down while players keep asking for more cards, each one a risk of going over 21.
pros: A player decides how much risk to take
The hidden card keeps the dealer's total unknown
cons: A player who goes over loses at once
The dealer wins ties, which tilts the game

source.ref: Spadaccini, S. (2005). The big book of rules: board games, kids' games, card games, from backgammon and bocce to tiddlywinks and stickball. New York: Plume. ISBN 978-0-452-28644-3.

pairs.tendency: In Euchre, the player who names trump may play alone, trusting one hand to win all five tricks for double points.
pros: Playing alone pays more if it works
The choice is the player's own, made from the cards in hand
cons: A lone hand leaves the partner out of the round
If the plan fails, the other side scores

source.ref: Spadaccini, S. (2005). The big book of rules: board games, kids' games, card games, from backgammon and bocce to tiddlywinks and stickball. New York: Plume. ISBN 978-0-452-28644-3.

pairs.tendency: In Bridge, one partner lays all their cards face up as the dummy, and the other partner plays both hands.
pros: The team plays with all its cards in view to one player
The opposing side sees one hand it can plan against
cons: One player does all the choosing for the team
The partner with the dummy only watches

source.ref: Spadaccini, S. (2005). The big book of rules: board games, kids' games, card games, from backgammon and bocce to tiddlywinks and stickball. New York: Plume. ISBN 978-0-452-28644-3.

pairs.tendency: Partners sit opposite each other and win tricks together, with no bidding. Each card played tells a partner something about the hand.
pros: Partners learn to read each other's plays.
Teamwork shows up in ordinary moves.
cons: One partner's plays can cost the whole team a trick.
Partners cannot see each other's cards.

source.ref: Spadaccini, S. (2005). The big book of rules: board games, kids' games, card games, from backgammon and bocce to tiddlywinks and stickball. New York: Plume. ISBN 978-0-452-28644-3.

pairs.tendency: Each player sees only their own cards, so the leader plays without knowing who can follow suit or trump.
pros: Every trick holds a small surprise.
Remembering played cards pays off.
cons: An uneven deal limits what a player can do.
Players who track every card may take longer on each play.

source.ref: Spadaccini, S. (2005). The big book of rules: board games, kids' games, card games, from backgammon and bocce to tiddlywinks and stickball. New York: Plume. ISBN 978-0-452-28644-3.

pairs.tendency: When you can only ask for what you already hold, each question shows other players part of your hand.
pros: Players learn to remember who asked for what.
Even young players can follow the rules.
cons: A player who forgets can lose track of the whole game.
Luck of the deal decides a lot.

source.ref: Spadaccini, S. (2005). The big book of rules: board games, kids' games, card games, from backgammon and bocce to tiddlywinks and stickball. New York: Plume. ISBN 978-0-452-28644-3.

pairs.tendency: Everyone pairs cards off and throws them away. The single unmatched card decides who loses, and nobody wins.
pros: Rounds are quick.
Everyone shares the same simple aim.
cons: Little skill is involved.
A player who loses often may stop wanting to play.

source.ref: Spadaccini, S. (2005). The big book of rules: board games, kids' games, card games, from backgammon and bocce to tiddlywinks and stickball. New York: Plume. ISBN 978-0-452-28644-3.

pairs.tendency: Cards are turned over one pair at a time, so each player sees where cards sit and has to remember it.
pros: Paying attention to others' turns matters.
Each turn gives away something.
cons: Players who forget fall behind.
A long game can drag if many cards stay hidden.

source.ref: Spadaccini, S. (2005). The big book of rules: board games, kids' games, card games, from backgammon and bocce to tiddlywinks and stickball. New York: Plume. ISBN 978-0-452-28644-3.

pairs.tendency: In rummy the first to empty their hand wins, so players get rid of high-value cards first in case someone else goes out.
pros: Early choices have a clear aim.
Taking from the discard pile shows others what you need.
cons: Players holding high cards late lose many points.
A player behind has few ways to catch up.

source.ref: Spadaccini, S. (2005). The big book of rules: board games, kids' games, card games, from backgammon and bocce to tiddlywinks and stickball. New York: Plume. ISBN 978-0-452-28644-3.

pairs.tendency: In Crazy Eights a player may keep a wild card back for the end, or draw extra cards to have more choices.
pros: Players can plan around luck.
Holding more cards sometimes gives more options.
cons: A player with an eight left when another wins loses many points.
A sudden end can leave a planner holding a wild card.

source.ref: Spadaccini, S. (2005). The big book of rules: board games, kids' games, card games, from backgammon and bocce to tiddlywinks and stickball. New York: Plume. ISBN 978-0-452-28644-3.

pairs.tendency: In Spit both players move at once and the hand ends in seconds. Quick eyes and hands decide who clears their cards first.
pros: Rounds are very short.
Players are always busy, with nobody waiting.
cons: Slower players often cannot keep up.
The game is hard to follow for onlookers.

source.ref: Spadaccini, S. (2005). The big book of rules: board games, kids' games, card games, from backgammon and bocce to tiddlywinks and stickball. New York: Plume. ISBN 978-0-452-28644-3.

pairs.tendency: In Slapjack players race to slap the pile and the fastest hand takes everything the others have put there.
pros: Reactions are easy to understand.
The winner of each slap is clear at once.
cons: A player with slow reactions may lose all their cards early.
Tied slaps need a rule to settle them.

source.ref: Spadaccini, S. (2005). The big book of rules: board games, kids' games, card games, from backgammon and bocce to tiddlywinks and stickball. New York: Plume. ISBN 978-0-452-28644-3.

pairs.tendency: In I Doubt It a player lays down cards while saying what they are, and plans which cards to play and when to tell the truth.
pros: Players plan the order of play.
A challenge early in the game lets a player fill gaps in their hand.
cons: A player can end up with many cards from one wrong challenge.
Honest plays near the end are easier to catch.

source.ref: Spadaccini, S. (2005). The big book of rules: board games, kids' games, card games, from backgammon and bocce to tiddlywinks and stickball. New York: Plume. ISBN 978-0-452-28644-3.

pairs.tendency: In poker each bet, call or raise can be a bluff, so players decide how much to risk on a hand others cannot see.
pros: Betting limits keep risk small.
Folding lets a player stop losing.
cons: A big bet can win a pot with a low-ranked hand.
Players who bluff often lose chips fast.

source.ref: Spadaccini, S. (2005). The big book of rules: board games, kids' games, card games, from backgammon and bocce to tiddlywinks and stickball. New York: Plume. ISBN 978-0-452-28644-3.
